items.title: Yusef Lateef — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: he taught uh the saxophonist Charles McPherson, from about age 13 somewhere, and Lonnie Hilliyer.

ctx.x: Uh could you talk about your um, your stints working with uh, with Barry Harris?

Oh, yes. Barry Harris is, is respected, highly respected, particularly in Detroit when we were all there, they called him the “high priest of music.” Um...he taught uh the saxophonist Charles McPherson, from about age 13 somewhere, and Lonnie Hilliyer. He’s a very wise man. In fact, I think I learned more about autophysiopsychic music from Barry than other one person, and he’s, he’s a world teacher right today. I respect him highly.

items.title: Charles McPherson interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: And we were recommended by Yusef, who worked with Mingus sometimes

ctx.x: Peter Stookey, right. No, it’s not, it’s Paul Stookey.

Well I knew him as Noel. Oh, okay. All right. Now he was just a folk singer singing, playing his guitar, and then we had this jam session in the afternoon, and Bill Cosby or people like that or even Bob Dylan would be at some coffee house across the street, and everybody was just like struggling nonentities basically, really. And so in the afternoon we’d have these sessions. And Mingus came by one afternoon because he was in need of an alto player and a trumpet player. And we were recommended by Yusef, who worked…

plucks them out with his hands. And so Lonnie and I, we looked at that and here we are, we’ve auditioned to get in this man’s band, and we’re in his band now, and there he is over there tearing the piano up, three hundred pounds. We were like 20 years old, 19, 20. And it was like oh, man, we work for somebody like this. And these gangsters, this just shows you the power of psychosis. I don’t care who anybody is, if you act, if you seem to be more crazy, crazier than they are, it’s awesome. And everybody respects…
